_doc: Schema: see docs/reference/api-parity-ledger/SCHEMA.md — the one home for what
a row means. Do NOT copy it back here; issue 1095 is what that cost.

c:allocator_t.why: rcl passes an `rcl_allocator_t` by value through most of its API so a caller can supply its own. nano-ros has ONE allocator, `nros_platform_alloc`, enforced by check-no-direct-kernel-alloc, so the type would only ever hold the same value. This is the `no-allocator` signature rule (signature_rules.py) one level up: the rule removes the parameter, this removes the type it would carry.

c:endpoint_info_t.why: phase-381 W3. The ours-half of the `topic_endpoint_info_array_t` divergence this file already records: upstream returns an allocating array, there is no allocator at this seam, and the endpoint count has no bound the CALLER can know. So it streams through a visitor, one entry of peak memory, every string borrowed for the call. The endpoint carries no QoS. The GRANTED profile is what answers 'why is nothing arriving', no backend can read one back yet, and reporting the remote's DECLARED profile would be a confident wrong answer -- so the field is absent here and the rmw ABI's `*_UNKNOWN` sentinels carry it at the vtable seam, which is that ABI's documented way to say 'could not determine'.

c:error_state_t.why: rcl keeps a thread-local error state with a formatted message, file and line, read back with rcl_get_error_string(). nano-ros returns `nros_ret_t` and nothing else -- there is no nros_error_string() and no per-thread error slot. What a C user loses is real and should be said plainly: a code, never a message. The constraint is thread-local storage plus a formatted-string buffer per thread, on targets where a task stack is measured in kilobytes.

c:error_string_t.why: the 1024-byte formatted buffer rcl_get_error_string() returns BY VALUE. Same decision as error_state_t; listed separately because it is the half a caller actually touches.

c:integrity_status_t.why: end-to-end safety telemetry per received sample -- sequence gap, duplicate flag, and a CRC verdict that distinguishes `no CRC on the wire` from `CRC mismatch`. RFC-0028. ROS 2 has no equivalent because a desktop DDS link is not treated as a safety channel; on a vehicle bus it is, and a receiver that cannot tell corruption from absence cannot implement a fail-silent reaction.

c:le_slice_view_f32_t.why: RFC-0033's C zero-copy reader, reachable from the umbrella header since issue 0795 was fixed. Borrows a view INTO the received CDR buffer instead of copying out of it: `nros_view_str_t` / `nros_view_bytes_t` for strings and byte arrays (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/view.h:39,45`), and the `nros_le_slice_view_*_t` family for numeric arrays, which are alignment-agnostic because CDR does not guarantee a `u64` array is 8-byte aligned in the wire buffer. ROS 2 has no counterpart: rosidl deserializes into an owned `std::vector`/`rosidl_runtime_c__*__Sequence`, which needs an allocator per message. The whole point here is that a subscription callback can read a 2 kB point cloud without a 2 kB copy it has nowhere to put. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this shared sentence named `nros_borrowed_str_t` / `nros_borrowed_bytes_t`, which exist nowhere in the tree; the types are `nros_view_str_t` / `nros_view_bytes_t`. Fixed in all 28 rows that carried the boilerplate, not just the one it was noticed on.

c:node_ref_t.why: phase-379 W4. rcl asks the caller to re-supply the node at teardown (`rcl_publisher_fini(&pub, &node)`); we keep `nros_publisher_fini(&pub)` and store this identity instead of the `*const nros_node_t` the entity used to hold. The PLATFORM constraint is that C gives the caller no tools to enforce the lifetime rcl's shape depends on: a node declared on an RTOS task stack dies with `vTaskDelete`, `nros_node_t a = b;` is legal and silent, and there is no allocator to hide an indirection behind. rcl's form does not remove that assumption, it relocates it to a caller who cannot check it either. An identity CAN be checked: `nros_node_fini` retires the slot's generation, so finalising an entity after its node returns NROS_RET_STALE_NODE instead of succeeding silently against caller storage the runtime does not own. Generation 0 is reserved so a zeroed struct never resolves.

c:transport_ops_t.why: a bring-your-own transport vtable (`open`/`close`/`write`/`read` + `abi_version` + `user_data`) so a board can supply its own link. rcl reaches the network through rmw and an installed middleware implementation, neither of which an MCU has; the vtable is how a board with a UART, a CAN controller or a vendor TCP stack participates at all.

cpp:ErrorCode.why: the code inside `nros::Result`. Same constraint as Result -- rclcpp's equivalent information lives in the exception TYPE, which -fno-exceptions removes.

cpp:Expected.why: value-or-error where rclcpp returns the value and throws on failure. Same no-exceptions constraint. Not `std::expected`: that is C++23 and the freestanding builds have no STL.

cpp:Future.why: rclcpp hands back a `std::shared_future` and drives it with `spin_until_future_complete`. `<future>` needs threads, an allocator and exceptions -- all three absent here -- so `nros::Future<T>` is a single-shot slot the caller polls (`is_ready`/`try_take`) or waits on by driving the executor, which is RFC-0021's rule that every blocking helper takes the executor.

cpp:FutureReturnCode.why: rclcpp's spin_until_future_complete returns {SUCCESS, INTERRUPTED, TIMEOUT}. We can express two: `ErrorCode::Ok` and `ErrorCode::Timeout` (result.hpp). There is no INTERRUPTED -- rclcpp means `the context was shut down while waiting`, and a ported caller that distinguishes shutdown from timeout cannot do so here. Not a divergence: nothing about no_std prevents a third code, nobody has added one. Phase 379 W3.

cpp:Result.why: rclcpp signals failure by throwing, so it needs no result type. nano-ros builds with -fno-exceptions on Zephyr, FreeRTOS and bare-metal (RFC-0018), so every fallible call returns `nros::Result` and NROS_TRY() early-returns it. The constraint is no exceptions; the type is what replaces them.

rust:DynamicMessageError.why: rclrs 0.7.0's dynamic-message surface: load a type's structure at RUNTIME by name and read or build a message without compiling against it. It needs the introspection typesupport library loaded from disk plus heap for the field table. An image links the types it uses; the same decision the pubsub stage records for rclcpp's `GenericPublisher`/`GenericSubscription`.

rust:Promise.why: RFC-0021: a `Promise` is what an async call returns, and every blocking helper takes the executor and drives it (`promise.wait(&mut executor, timeout)`). rclrs returns a future and needs a runtime to await it; rclcpp returns a `std::shared_future` and drives it through `spin_until_future_complete`. part of the IMPERATIVE Rust API, which coexists with the declarative component model and is the rclrs-shaped one: `NodeHandle` (exported from `nros` and IN THE PRELUDE, behind `rmw-cffi`) hands back concrete entities you hold and call. rclrs's counterpart exists and correlates by concept but not by name, because ours carries the storage strategy in the type -- `Embedded*` means the entity lives in the executor's static table rather than behind an `Arc`, which is the no-allocator constraint made visible in the name. Whether the two Rust APIs should both be public, and which one `nros::` should lead with, is issue 0784.

Whether the two Rust APIs should both be public, and which one `nros::` should lead with, is issue 0784.

rust:RclErrorMsg.why: the owned String rclrs copies out of rcl's thread-local error state. Same decision as the C `error_string_t`, and the same constraint: no per-thread formatted-message buffer. A `no_std` build has no String either.

rust:RclReturnCode.why: the `rcl_ret_t` numeric mirror rclrs's error carries. Was a `gap` here, on the reading that we had the type (nros-core/src/error.rs) and merely failed to export it. Issue 0783 settled it the other way and DELETED it, because exporting it would have shipped a type a user can name and never receive: nothing in the tree produced an `RclReturnCode`, its only appearance was as the `code` field of `NanoRosError` (see `rust:RclrsError`), and its numeric space is not ours -- our codes are `NROS_RET_*`, 0 and -1..-16, an independent negative space defined in nros-c/src/error.rs and reached only across the C/C++ ABI. The Rust user API matches a flat enum and carries no numeric code at any layer, which is the divergence `rust:RclrsError` records. Constraint: `no_std` (a code table is not the cost -- the absent thread-local error state it indexes into is).

rust:RclrsError.why: rclrs's error is source-chained, carries an owned `RclErrorMsg` copied out of rcl's thread-local error state, and implements std::error::Error. `no_std` has neither the per-thread formatted-message buffer nor the allocation for a chain, so ours is a flat `nros::NodeError` enum whose most common variant is `NodeError::Transport(TransportError)` -- both exported unconditionally, and now from ONE block in the facade (issue 0783). We do implement `core::error::Error` (phase-359), so that half is not a divergence any more. RETRACTED, and this row carried the wrong version for a while: issue 0783 originally said `TransportError` was not exported, so a caller could hold the error and not match its contents. It IS exported, at packages/api/nros/src/lib.rs, and was throughout; the real finding was that the two halves of the vocabulary sat in unrelated re-export blocks. See the same correction in other.json's `rust:TransportError`.

rust:RclrsErrorFilter.why: an iterator adapter over `Result` that swallows take-failed and timeout as non-errors. It exists because rclrs's take path reports an empty queue as an error; ours reports emptiness as `Ok(false)` (issue 0757's audit), so there is nothing to filter.

rust:TakeFailedAsNone.why: rclrs/src/error.rs, not its action model -- this row previously said `part of its action/goal model, see rust:AcceptedGoal`, which was a mis-file: the trait turns a take that failed into `Ok(None)`. It exists because rclrs's take path reports an empty queue as an ERROR; ours reports emptiness as `Ok(false)` / `None` (issue 0757's audit), so there is nothing to convert back. Same decision and same reason as `rust:RclrsErrorFilter`. We DID carry a copy -- phase-16 cloned both traits into nros-core/src/error.rs against `NanoRosError` -- and issue 0783 deleted it with the error type it was written for: no fallible call in the user API ever returned that error, so the adapter had no `Result` to adapt.

rust:TakeFailedAsNone::take_failed_as_no.why: the trait's only method; see `rust:TakeFailedAsNone`. Ours reports an empty take as `Ok(false)` / `None` directly, so there is no take-failed error to convert.
